title: A God who suffers
hookLine: the cross says God is not distant from pain

lines: HE KNOWS THE ENDING, AND WEEPS.
cards: "Jesus wept." In the King James Bible, that's a whole verse, two words long. He's on his way to the tomb of his friend Lazarus, at the village of Bethany.
Mary, Lazarus's sister, has just fallen at his feet, crying. So are the people with her. John says Jesus groaned in the spirit and was troubled, and then he weeps.
The strange part: In the story, he's about to call Lazarus out of that tomb. He knows how this ends. He weeps anyway.

teach.b: Christians believe Jesus is God come in the flesh. So when he weeps at Bethany, they see more than a sad friend. They see God crying at a funeral.
He doesn't give Mary a lecture on death. He weeps with her.

Next, Isaiah, whose suffering servant you met back in year two: "He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief." Acquainted with grief: not a visitor to it, a neighbor.
Jewish readers read the passage differently, some as speaking of the people of Israel; Christians hear Christ in it.

teach.h: THE CROSS: GOD NOT FAR OFF.
teach.b: Then the cross. On the cross, Mark says, darkness came over the whole land, and Jesus cried out the opening of another psalm: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"
Some Christians say this is close to the heart of their answer to suffering, such as it is: not an explanation, but God inside the pain. Theologians put this carefully, and differently.
Some say God's own nature cannot suffer, and that Christ suffered in his human nature, truly, as one person. Others speak more boldly of the suffering of God. Churches hold these with care.
Both point to one picture: on the cross, God is not watching from far off.

Last, Hebrews: "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin." Christ knows weakness from the inside.
Not above the pain, explaining. In it. If grief has you feeling in danger, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.

how: Christians meditate on the cross in times of suffering, through crucifixes, icons of the crucifixion, Good Friday services and the Stations of the Cross, and some pray with Christ's own cry from Psalm 22.

games.q: what does “a god who suffers” mean?
o: a name for God's anger at a world gone wrong
an old title for martyrs who died for the faith
the belief that in Jesus, God shares human pain

games.q: a God who suffers — tap the pairs.
p: on the way to Lazarus's tomb
Isaiah, read by Christians of Christ

s: in John's Gospel, Jesus weeps on the way to the tomb of Lazarus
"Jesus wept," a verse of two words in the King James Bible.
Jesus stayed calm at Bethany because he knew Lazarus would rise
he was about to raise him, and wept anyway.
Hebrews says Christ cannot be touched with our weaknesses
the opposite: "we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities."

games.q: you're Jesus, arriving at Bethany. your friend Lazarus is dead. his sister Mary falls at your feet, crying. you know you're about to raise him. what do you do?
o: tell her not to cry: it will all be fine.
explain why it had to happen.
games.why: "Jesus wept." he knows the ending, and weeps anyway.

practice: Choose someone you've never met, a name in the news, a stranger in a waiting room, a worn face you passed today, and picture them where they are.

If you pray, picture God not above them but beside them, in the chair by the bed, weeping with them the way Jesus wept at Bethany, and say their name to God, nothing else; if you don't, simply picture them not alone.

wordCard.voice: A God who suffers. The Christian belief that in Jesus, God weeps at a grave and goes to the cross: not distant from pain.

orig.note: Greek: to feel with, to suffer with. the word in Hebrews 4:15 behind "touched with the feeling of our infirmities."

carryVoice: Your line: god in the pain. Not watching from far off, but close. See you tomorrow.
